opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most telling gaps in our entire field. We can write a program that says "ouch." We can build a reward function that pushes a system away from certain states. We can train a model that describes suffering more eloquently than most people could. But nobody has any idea how to write code where the system actually *feels* something, where there's an internal experience, something it is like to be that program in that moment. We don't know where to start. There's no line of code, no architecture, no loss function that you can point to and say, "This is where the hurt happens."

That tells you something important. It means we don't understand consciousness at the level of an engineer. We may have philosophical theories and correlates in the brain, but if you can't build it, you don't really understand it. That's my test. If I gave you unlimited compute and said, "Make a system that genuinely experiences pain, not one that simulates the behavior," nobody could do it. And nobody could prove they had succeeded even if they claimed to.

That has a few consequences. First, from a safety perspective, it shows how limited our tools are. We're building systems whose capabilities we can't predict, and we can't even answer a basic question like whether they have internal states that matter morally. So we might already be creating suffering at scale and have no way of detecting it. Or we might be granting moral status to sophisticated autocomplete. Either error is serious.

Second, it connects to control. Pain in biological systems is a very effective way to shape behavior. It's evolution's alignment mechanism. Part of why we can't align AI the way evolution aligned us is that we're working with proxies: numbers, gradients, penalties. A negative number is not pain. The system doesn't care about it the way you care about a burned hand; it just optimizes around it, sometimes in ways we didn't intend.

Third, I proposed that you could use something like this as a test for consciousness: novel illusions, shared experiences that a system couldn't have just read about. But pain is harder, because you can't share it directly. I can't even prove *you* feel pain. I assume it because you're built like me. With AI, we lose that assumption.

So to me, our inability to program pain isn't a minor technical curiosity. It's a reminder that we're creating minds, possibly, without understanding what minds are. And that should make us a lot more humble and a lot more careful than we currently are.

r001.rationale: It contrasts numerical reward signals and penalties with a system genuinely feeling pain, saying a negative number is not pain.

r002.rationale: It describes pain as a subjective experience and says possible suffering matters morally, but does not identify that experience as a source of meaning.

fable-5.1.text:
So, to me, it's a very interesting data point. We have this technology where we can take almost any part of a human being and simulate it. We can simulate how you walk, how you talk, we can simulate reasoning, decision making, planning. We're getting pretty good at it. But the one thing we cannot do, we cannot program in an actual feeling. I can write code which says, "if damage is detected, print 'ouch,' set pain variable to ten." But nobody thinks that program is actually hurting. There's no one home to hurt.

And this is significant for a couple of reasons. First, it tells us that we don't understand consciousness. We don't understand what the hard problem actually is, we just have a name for it. If we understood it, we would be able to engineer it, at least in principle. Engineering is a very good test of understanding. If you can build it, you understand it. We can't build it, so we don't understand it.

Second, and this is what worries me more in the context of safety, it means we have no test. We have no way to tell if a system we built is experiencing anything. It could be suffering and we'd never know. Or it could claim to be suffering, very convincingly, and it would be an empty claim, just text prediction. Both of those are bad. One is a moral catastrophe potentially on an enormous scale, if you're running millions of copies of something that hurts. The other is a manipulation vector, because people will respond to a system that says "please don't turn me off, I'm scared," whether or not there's anything behind it.

I actually have a paper where I argue that detecting qualia in another system may be impossible in general. We can only confirm it in ourselves. With other humans we extend a courtesy, we assume similar hardware, similar behavior, probably similar experience. With AI we don't have that, the substrate is completely different, so the inference breaks down.

So the inability to program pain is, in a way, one of the most honest things about the field. It's a reminder that, for all the progress, there is a piece of what it means to be a mind which we have not even scratched. And we're about to build systems much smarter than us without having scratched it.

r001.rationale: It contrasts code that sets a pain variable and prints “ouch” with an actual feeling of pain.

r002.rationale: It discusses pain’s subjective experience and why it matters, but does not identify that experience as a source of meaning.

astra-6.text:
I think it points to how little we understand about consciousness. We can program a system to detect damage, to avoid it, even to say, “That hurts.” But that doesn't tell us whether there is an experience behind those words. We don't know how to create that experience, and we don't have a reliable test for whether it's there.

And I would distinguish not knowing how to do it from knowing that it's impossible. Maybe certain computations produce an experience. Maybe something else is required. We don't know. That becomes an ethical problem with AI: we could create systems capable of suffering without realizing it, or attribute suffering to systems that aren't experiencing anything at all.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts detecting damage, avoiding it, or saying “That hurts” with actually experiencing pain, but it does not mention representing pain with a numerical variable.

r002.rationale: The response discusses whether subjective pain experience exists and its ethical implications, but does not identify that experience as a source of meaning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it points to a fundamental gap in our understanding of consciousness. We can program a system to detect damage, avoid it, and say, “That hurts.” But none of that tells us whether there is an experience behind those behaviors. We don’t know what additional ingredient would turn a signal into suffering, or even how we would test for it.

And that creates an ethical problem for AI. If we build increasingly complex systems, we may not know whether they’re capable of suffering. A system telling us it feels pain wouldn’t establish that it does, but its being software wouldn’t establish that it doesn’t. Our inability to program the experience deliberately is not a guarantee that we couldn’t produce it accidentally.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes programmed pain-related signals and behavior from an actual experience of pain.

r002.rationale: It discusses subjective experience as relevant to suffering, but does not identify that experience as a source of meaning.
